RE: House Bill 1396
Dear Co-Chairs Beebe-Center and Hasenfus, and Members of the Joint Criminal Justice & Public Safety Committee,
As the advocacy voice of the responsible pet care community, the Pet Advocacy Network represents the interests and expertise of retailers, companion animal suppliers, manufacturers, distributors, pet owners, and others involved in the many aspects of pet care across the United States. Our association promotes animal well-being and responsible pet ownership, fosters environmental stewardship, and ensures healthy pets' availability through our local, state, and federal work. In addition, we routinely advocate for legislative and regulatory proposals to protect the health, safety, and availability of companion animals.
On behalf of the responsible pet care community, we ask that you vote YES on House Bill 1396, which would provide healthcare cost reimbursement for retired law enforcement canines.
Law enforcement canines are indispensable members of our public safety community. They are highly trained officers who serve alongside their human partners in some of the most dangerous and demanding situations imaginable. These canines track missing persons, locate narcotics and explosives, apprehend dangerous suspects, and protect both officers and the public. They run toward danger, enter unknown environments first, and absorb risks that would otherwise fall to their human partners.
A K-9's retirement marks the end of active duty, not the end of the physical toll that duty has taken. Many retired K-9s experience service-related injuries, joint deterioration, and other medical conditions that require ongoing veterinary treatment. Unlike the officers they serve beside, retired K-9s do not receive pensions or guaranteed health benefits. Their handlers or adoptive families assume full financial responsibility for their care.
This legislation is both compassionate and responsible. By establishing the Retired Law Enforcement K-9 Health Care Fund within the Department of Public Safety, Maine would provide up to $5,000 in lifetime veterinary reimbursement for eligible retired law enforcement canines. This is a modest but meaningful investment that recognizes their service and helps offset the financial burden placed on handlers and adopters.
Importantly, the bill: � Clearly defines eligibility standards to ensure funds are used appropriately. � Limits reimbursement to documented veterinary expenses. � Caps reimbursement at $5,000 per canine, subject to available appropriations. � Allows agencies the discretion to provide additional support from their own budgets. � Permits private donations and grants to supplement public funding.

This framework ensures accountability, flexibility, and fiscal responsibility. This bill sends a powerful message: Maine values all members of its law enforcement community, including the K-9 officers who serve alongside them. Providing assistance for their medical care is a matter of honoring their sacrifice and ensuring they can live their retirement years with dignity and quality of life. Other states have recognized the importance of similar programs. Delaware, Florida, and Illinois have enacted similar laws in recent years. Connecticut, Massachusetts, North Carolina, South Carolina, and Pennsylvania all currently have similar legislation under consideration. Maine now has the opportunity to demonstrate leadership and compassion while supporting the dedicated handlers who often adopt their retired partners. These canines have spent their lives protecting our communities. Supporting this bill is a simple and meaningful way for us to protect them in return. We respectfully urge the committee to vote YES on HB 1396. Thank you for your time and consideration, Alisa Clements Director, Government Affairs

Testimony in support of LD 2081

February 9, 2026

Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus, and members of the Criminal Justice and Public
Safety Committee,

My name is

I live in Scarborough, and I am a Senior Fire Investigator at The Office of

State Fire Marshal. In that capacity I served as a K9 handler for the State of Maine from 2016

through 2023 with my partner, K9 Deacon, a yellow labrador retriever. Deacon is now 12 years old

and retired. He lives with my family and is, thankfully, in generally good health.

Being a working dog takes a toll. Years of high-impact work, repeatedly jumping in and out of vehicles, operating in dangerous environments, harsh weather, and unpredictable fire scenes, create long-term physical strain that often doesn't fully present until after retirement.

Although Deacon is no longer working, retirement does not erase the years of service he gave to the
State of Maine. It has been a great privilege to bring him into my home as part of my family.
However, from the beginning, there was always the potential that his service could result in significant veterinary costs later in life, which can be costly for any family to manage.

When fire investigators retire in good standing, the State recognizes their service by continuing
health-related benefits. There are currently presumptive laws that provide workers compensation benefits for both police officers and firefighters that acknowledge the cost of service does not end
on the last day of work. Extending similar consideration to our retired working K9s, who served under the same hazardous conditions, is a matter of consistency and respect for the role they played as living, breathing members of ourteams.

I understood the risks and the potential financial responsibility when I accepted the role of handler. But I would hate to see a future, highly qualified and motivated candidate hesitate, or decline entirely, because of uncertainty about the long-term care of a retired working dog.

This bill does not guarantee payment for unnecessary or frivolous expenses. It simply gives the chief officer the discretion to evaluate legitimate veterinary needs and approve coverage when
appropriate.

Realistically, the amount of time during which I may personally benefit from this change is likely
short, if at all. Sadly, a 12 year old dog often sees his best years behind him. But future handlers will
face the same challenges I have faced, and their decisions will shape the strength of these
programs moving forward. For those reasons, I respectfully urge the committee to vote in favor of
this bill.

Respectfully submitted,

LD 2081- An Act to Provide Health Care Cost Reimbursement for Retired Law
Enforcement Canines
Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus, and members of the Criminal Justice and Public
Safety Committee, my name is Shawn Esler, and I am honored to serve as Maine's State Fire `""`""--"""")
Marshal.
I am here today to testify in support of LD 2081, a bill that reflects the real-world experience of
agencies that rely on law enforcement K-9s and the reality faced by handlers once those dogs retire. For the State Fire Marshal's Office, this issue is personal.
Our office has operated an accelerant detection K-9 program since 1991 and we currently have three active labrador retrievers. However, today we are here to discuss our retired K-9s (Harry and Deacon) who previously served the State of Maine in that capacity. Together, they supported
hundreds of fire and arson investigations across Maine and the Northeast, working alongside local, state, and federal partners on complex cases.
Throughout their careers, Harry and Deacon were deployed to fire scenes to locate ignitable liquids, allowing investigators to pinpoint evidence, confirm laboratory results, and strengthen criminal prosecutions. Beyond investigative work, both dogs contributed to federal training efforts, fire prevention education, school visits, and extensive community outreach, participating in hundreds of public demonstrations and events statewide. These dogs have become the face of our agency and are considered an essential part of our operations.
Currently both K-9s are retired after years of active law enforcement service and now face the
reality of age-related and service-related medical needs like mobility issues, cancer, and lung problems that require ongoing veterinary care. These issues are exacerbated, likely because of lifelong exposure to carcinogens found at every fire scene. Once a K-9 retires, those medical costs are no longer covered by the State or agency. Despite years of public service, financial
responsibility shifts entirely to the handler, both of whom are still actively serving our office.
LD 2081 addresses this gap in a responsible and measured way. It establishes a Retired Law
Enforcement K-9 Health Care Fund with clear eligibility criteria, defined reimbursable expenses, and a reasonable lifetime cap, with additional reimbursement decisions subject to the discretion and approval of the agency head or chief. This is not an open-ended benefit, it is a targeted, accountable program that recognizes the service these animals provide while maintaining
appropriate oversight.

resource, helps with recruitment and retention of K-9 handlers, and sends a clear message that Maine values service beyond the end of active duty. I understand the state budget constraints and concerns around spending. From a fiscal standpoint, I would support a zero-dollar fiscal note simply to establish a statutory pathway for reimbursement. Creating the framework does not require appropriation, but it allows flexibility
for future funding through philanthropic organizations, fundraising efforts, court-ordered
restitution, and contributions from individual departments when operating budgets allow. This approach ensures fiscal restraint while still providing a transparent and accountable mechanism to support retired law enforcement K-9s only when resources are available.
While LD 2081 contains expanded language to include other State law enforcement departments,
this is a real problem facing the Fire Marshal's Office. Therefore, I respectfully urge the

Good afternoon Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfuss, and members of
the Criminal Justice Committee.
Maine has partnered with K9s in law enforcement since the late l97Os. These highly trained dogs provide services that human officers simply cannot. K9s can
detect hidden dangers, alert officers to specific substances, and provide critical
support, especially in Maine's most rural and remote areas.
Law enforcement officers who enroll in K9 programs make a significant personal commitment by bringing a trained police K9 into their homes. These dogs require
constant training and must consistently meet rigorous performance standards.
Living and working together day in and day out, the handler and K9 develop a
deep bond built on trust, loyalty, and shared service throughout their careers.
`
At the end of a K9's career, it is common for the handler to honor that loyalty by
adopting the dog into retirement, assuming full responsibility for its care at their
own expense. However, the medical and care costs associated with a retired police
K9, often shaped by years of demanding service, can be significant. This bill establishes an accountable, donation-supported fund to help support these valuable
K9 partners and the families who care for them, ensuring they receive the respect
and care they have earned through years of service to our state.
Thank you.

House District 17 Orland, Penobscot, Verona Island, and Bucksport
